rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous unknowns as questions, not fake certainty. "Brands get paid on day one. Who carries the 60-day float?" is the right kind of sharp: it gives a reporter a real economics question and names the proof required. B has useful bones, but "Faire absorbs all the default risk" and "no bank required" are courtroom-confidence claims built on facts the update does not give.
gaps_in_A: "cash flow, not demand" is sharper than the supplied facts support; the update says cash flow is the top barrier, not that demand is irrelevant.
"rather than a bank score" goes a step beyond the update; it says Faire uses order history, not that it excludes bank scores, credit bureaus, or partners.
"A $12.6B marketplace decides its next product is credit" is viable, but only if the valuation date and revenue-versus-subsidy answer are nailed down before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "no bank required" is invented. The update says Faire underwrites using order history; it does not say there is no bank partner, credit facility, or outside capital.
"Faire absorbs all the default risk" is the worst overreach in the set. Default risk and financing-cost terms are explicitly not disclosed.
"700,000 retailer order histories" turns marketplace size into product coverage and data depth. The update gives 700,000 retailers, not 700,000 eligible borrowers with usable histories.
"Faire isn't using a credit bureau" and "purchase frequency" add underwriting details the update never supplied. That is not color; that is making stuff up.
